_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 7 specification: four sections A–D, ten questions, each section the answer two or three times. Every question paraphrases its section, and several have a near-miss in another section (Rosa's cheap keys vs Agnieszka's free finds; Desmond's talks vs Agnieszka's shoebox). Used by the Part 7 practice page.
title: It started with one
subtitle: Four people talk about their unusual collections.

sections.A: Rosa, 52, dentist. When I was eleven, my grandmother gave me the front-door key of the house she'd grown up in, which had been knocked down years before. I was fascinated by the idea of a key with no door, and I've been collecting old keys ever since. I now have about four hundred, mounted in frames all along the hallway, and I've never paid more than a few pounds for any of them; most come from junk shops and car-boot sales. What I love is imagining the doors they once opened: a prison cell, a church, somebody's garden shed. My husband calls the hallway 'the dungeon', but he puts up with it. A few years ago, when we were short of space, I sorted out a big box to sell online. I photographed every one, then put them all back on the wall. I just couldn't do it.
sections.B: Finn, 16, school student. It began on a school trip to Belgium, when I put two sugar sachets from a café in my pocket and forgot about them. Back home I noticed how nice the designs were, and somehow, three years later, I've got more than two thousand. My friends think it's hilarious. The thing is, I hardly ever travel, so nearly all of them are brought back by aunts, uncles and family friends, who now raid every café they visit on holiday. My dad eventually had to put up a special shelf in my room. Every sachet goes into a spreadsheet with its country, the date and where it came from, which sounds sad, but it means I know exactly what I've got. Last year I did a swap by post with a collector in Japan: fifty British ones for fifty of his. His were much better.
sections.C: Agnieszka, 39, librarian. My collection isn't really something I chose. Over fifteen years of working in a public library, I've found all kinds of things left inside returned books: shopping lists, bus tickets, pressed flowers, a child's drawing of a very angry cat, even a twenty-pound note, which I handed in. Every single item came to me for free, which is probably the only way a librarian could afford a hobby. Most of them I keep in a shoebox under my desk at home. My favourite is a letter that begins 'Dear Margaret, I'm sorry about the goat' and then stops. Once I found a wedding photograph with names on the back, and after weeks of searching I managed to post it back to the couple. They wrote to thank me. People tell me I should write a blog about the box, and perhaps one day I will.
sections.D: Desmond, 74, retired engineer. I bought my first egg cup, shaped like a chicken wearing a hat, at a seaside shop in 1972, and I now own just over twelve hundred. For decades they lived in glass cabinets in the dining room, until my wife told me, very kindly, that it was either her or the egg cups. They're in the garage now, which I've fitted out with shelves and lights. Some are quite valuable, the most expensive one being worth about three hundred pounds, but that's never been the point for me. I've given talks to the local history society and to a couple of primary schools, and the children always want to know which one I eat my boiled egg from. What does worry me is the future. My grandchildren are lovely, but I suspect the whole lot will end up in a skip.

questions.question: Which person has never had to pay for any items in their collection?
questions.why: 'Every single item came to me for free.' Rosa has paid for her keys, even if only 'a few pounds'.

questions.question: Which person depends on others to add to their collection?
questions.why: 'Nearly all of them are brought back by aunts, uncles and family friends.'

questions.question: Which person was unable to part with items they had planned to get rid of?
questions.why: She sorted out a box to sell, 'then put them all back on the wall. I just couldn't do it.'

questions.question: Which person had to relocate their collection because of a family member?
questions.why: His wife said 'it was either her or the egg cups. They're in the garage now.' Finn's dad put up a shelf, but nothing was moved.

questions.question: Which person keeps a detailed record of what they own?
questions.why: 'Every sachet goes into a spreadsheet with its country, the date and where it came from.'

questions.question: Which person managed to return an item to the people it belonged to?
questions.why: After weeks of searching she 'managed to post it back to the couple'.

questions.question: Which person is anxious about what will become of their collection?
questions.why: 'What does worry me is the future… the whole lot will end up in a skip.'

questions.question: Which person became interested in collecting because of a present from an older relative?
questions.why: Her grandmother 'gave me the front-door key of the house she'd grown up in'. Finn's relatives supply sachets, but they did not start his hobby.

questions.question: Which person has spoken about their collection to audiences?
questions.why: 'I've given talks to the local history society and to a couple of primary schools.' Agnieszka has only been told she should write a blog.

questions.question: Which person has exchanged items with someone in another country?
questions.why: 'I did a swap by post with a collector in Japan.'
